title: Earth Is Lumpy as Hell
gist: NASA has released a geoid image built from more than a billion observations by 19 satellites, showing Earth's gravitational field rather than its surface, with height exaggerated 10,000 times to make the lumpiness visible.

insights.claim: NASA's new geoid image of Earth was compiled from more than a billion observations collected by 19 satellites.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Billion-observation multi-satellite geodesy shows how much of modern Earth science now depends on constellation-scale orbital infrastructure rather than single missions.
insights.quote: compiled from more than a billion observations from 19 satellites
insights.locator: it’s an image of what Earth’s gravitational field

insights.claim: The geoid depicts the shape Earth's oceans would take if every fissure and trench were filled and every mountain sanded down, making it a map of the gravitational field rather than a photograph of the planet.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Distinguishing gravitational shape from physical shape is the conceptual basis for satellite altimetry and precise sea-level measurement.
insights.quote: If you were somehow able to fill all the fissures and trenches with spackle and sand down the mountains, this is the (again, exaggerated) shape the ocean would take.

insights.claim: The geoid's visible lumpiness is an artifact of deliberate visualization choices, with geoid height exaggerated by a factor of 10,000 for effect.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A 10,000x exaggeration is a reminder that scientific imagery that goes viral is usually rescaled, and headline visuals should be checked against the underlying magnitudes.
insights.quote: The Geoid, with the geoid height exaggerated by a factor of 10,000.

insights.claim: The Apollo 17 crew's "Blue Marble" photo, showing Earth from the South Pole to the Mediterranean Sea, set the aesthetic reference point that the far less flattering geoid image now contrasts against.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Public engagement with Earth science still runs through a single 1972 image, which is why agencies keep investing in visualization as much as in data.
insights.locator: As the crew of Apollo 17 zoomed toward the moon
